div.head: Again the book of the Song of Songs, and there are in it two sections.

div.ab:
Firstly proem. The pious preceptors, Gregorius of Nyssa and Chrysostom and Hippolytus interpreted this book as (having reference) to the human soul which is longing for divine communion, while Theodorus, the exegete of the Nestorians, said that Solomon praised with these words the daughter of Pharaoh who was black and was being found fault with by the Hebrew women, so that the peace between him and her father should not be broken and dissolved. For he even took her out of Jerusalem and settled her in that great house which he had built for her in the Mount Lebanon for this (same) reason. But that this opinion is incorrect is made evident by the fact that, even though Solomon had not been the king but (merely) one of the common people, he would have been ashamed to say about his wife, that she roamed about at night in the streets (3:2) and that the guards took her and bruised her (5:7); nor again would he have permitted (himself) to extol her thighs (7:1) and her navel (7:2). The Jews,however, even
though (they are) extreme literalistselevate its scope as (being) from their congregation toward God. Others, however, (make it refer) to Abishag the Shilumite, because she is mentioned in it.

div.head: Section One.
div.ab: First Section. Some read Sherath Sherin with Rebaso of Shin and 'Alaf, but in old manuscripts (it is written) with Hebhas of Shin and Jodh, Shirath Shirin, i. e., Song of Songs. (1:1) He kissed me, as in the past tense; the Greek reads he will kiss me, as in the future tense. Since the bride is a spiritual one, she is not ashamed to say these (words) to the bridegroom, God, her lord; for the physical one would be ashamed to reveal her desire. For they love is better than wine, i. e., thy love gladdens more than wine. And the Greek says, because thy breasts are good, i. e., your teachings which are nourishing to me like milk to the body. (1:2)Oil of myrrh is thy name, i. e., mention of thee is sweet, the maidens love thee, i. e., the rational sould. (1:3) And from the upright, i. e., angels and saintly men. (1:4) I am black but I am comely, i. e., although I am spotted with sins, yet my origin is from God.

Kedar, i. e., darkness. (1:5) For the sun blackened me, i. e., my blackness is accidental, and I was not created with a spotted nature. My mother's children strove against me, i. e., corporeal forces,passion and desire, they made me
keeper of the vineyards, i. e., guardian of the corporeal organs. But my own vineyard have I not kept, i. e., I was captivated by lusts. (1:8) If thou knowest not thyself, i. e., if thou doest not regard thy glory, thy beloved will not be shown to thee. Come thou in the footsteps of the flock, i. e., direct the natural forces of generation, rearing, and nourishing, and pasture thy kids, beside (Lit: in) the shepherd's tents, i. e., while the bad (Lit: left handed) thoughts which are wanton with thee are still small, subdue them by the regulations that the prophets and the apostles and the fathers have laid down for thee. (1:9) To my mare in Pharaoh's chariot I have compared thee; i. e., thou, oh soul, if you will not curb yourself from the waywardness of your course, you will become like the chariot of Pharaoh when you will sink into the sea of passions. (1:9) Thy cheeks are comely with tresses and thy neck with strings of beads; i. e., in thy virtues are thy ornaments. (1:10) thin plates, i. e., crescents. (1:13) A cluster of henna flowers, i. e., of
henna. My beloved in the vineyard of En-gedi; i. e., the discerning soul calls the Lord her father's brother, since he has called her parents the holy apostles, his brothers. Thus said our commentators; but in my opinion the noun dada is derived from jedhidha, that is to say, beloved and with this the Hebrew agrees, but the Greek says the son of my sister, since her beloved was born in the flesh from the congregation of the (chosen) people, which is the older sister of our congregation; and the vineyard of En-gedi is a type of the splendor of the heavens (studded) with stars as with blossoms. (1:15) Thine eyes are those of doves, i. e., in innocence.

(2:2) As a lily among thorns; i. e., a discerning soul among foolish souls. (1:16) Although our couch is crowded (with Hewas of Sadhe), but in old manuscripts 2-s-f They brought me into the winehouse, i. e., into the house of
gladdening instruction. And arrange love for (Lit: upon) me, i. e., for our God is love. (2:7) By the gazelles and by the antelopes of the fields, i. e., by the free soulsthat are not shackled by material fetters. That you will not stir up nor awaken the Hebrew 'em tairu w 'em teuru, i. e., I am adjuring you that you shall neither admonish nor reproach, for neither by admonition nor by reproach is my love distraught. (2:8) The voice of my father's brother, i. e., tidings of him aforetime the prophets proclaimed to me. Behold this is he who comes, i. e., at the end when he is made flesh. (2:9) Behold he stands behind our wall, i. e., after the Mosaic law,which was put up as a hedge. Looking forth at the
windows, straining through the lattices; i. e., it was foretold by the revelations and visions of the prophets. (2:11) For the winter is past, i. e., the time of coldness of the love of God in those who were quickly inclining towards idolatry. And the rain has past,i. e., the hampering shadows of the law. (2:12) The flowers have appeared on the land, i. e., because the sun of righteousness has drawn near. The time of pruning is come; i. e., the separation of the good from the evil. And the voice of the turtle dove is heard in our land, i. e., the voice of that one calling in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord. (2:13) The fig tree has put forth (Lit.: given) its buds, i. e., prophecy has revealed its secrets. Paque are the buds of the fig
trees. Semadre are the flowers of the grapevine. (2:13c) And come (2:14) my dove into the clefts of the rock; i. e., by means of the aural orifices which receive the teaching, be guided to me in the coverts (of the hedge); i. e., from the recesses of the heart and brain. (2:15) Take us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vineyard; i. e., demoniacal illusions that cause the body to be wanton. And vineyard of vine shoots; i. e., as the form of the shoot rises up above the rest of the plant formations so the organ (of) human generation above the rest of the organs. (2:16) Who pastures in the lilies; i. e., rests in the works of the righteous. (2:17) Until the day grows cool, and the shadows fall, i. e., until the end, and then he will pay every man according to his deeds.

(3:1) On my bed in the night I sought him whom my soul loves; i. e., even in dreams she yearned for him. I sought him but I found him not; i. e., because only the perfect mind find him, but imagination do not attain him. (3:2) I will arise now and go about the cities in the streets and the squares, i. e., perhaps from the creation I will recognize the creator. (3:2) The watchman found me; i. e., carnal forces. (3:4) It was but a little that I passed from them; i. e., when I passed from the path of the senses to the
road of reason then I was guided aright and I found him. I held him and would not let loose until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that gave birth to me, i. e., house he calls the heart and mother and parturient (he calls) wisdom. (3:6) Who is this that comes out of the wilderness; i. e., the soul which departs from the body like a vapor of smoke, i. e., little by little it is cleared of the material darkness perfumed with myrrh, i. e., with the mortification of the body. Behold the bed of Solomon, sixty valiant men surround it; i. e., five armed men from each tribe were guarding the bed of Solomon, for twelve times five makes sixty. And Saint Hippolytius of Rome explains those sixty valiants spiritually as (representing) the personalities that begin with Adam and end with Joseph, and he said that by these was guarded the holy bed of the Virgin, the mother of the heavenly bridegroom; but seventy-five did this and not sixty. (3:11) With the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding; i. e., with the crown of humility which wisdom put on him as he became flesh and bethrothed unto him the new church.

(4:1) Thy hair is as a flock of goats, i. e., the abundance of thy chastity, because the hair is an honor for women who acknowledge the fear of God as Paul said, that rose
up from Gilead, i. e., that departest from the worship of idols. (4:2) Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, i. e., white sheep whose hair is shorn and whose color is shining white, but in the manuscript of Michael it is written gzero dagzirtho, that is to say, instead of the last zain a single vowelless res but it is not correct; all of them bear twins; i. e., all their children are twins; and thoughts he compared to teeth for as the body (is nourished) by means of the teeth, so the soul is nourished by means of pure and unfailing thoughts. (4:3) Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely, i. e., delicate and excellent thoughts art thou uttering. Like the rind of pomegranates is thy neck, because of thy silence, i. e., like seeds which are hidden within peeling, so are thy words in thy mouth when you are silent. (4:4) Like the tower of David is thy neck built with necklaces, i. e., the desires are so high. (4:5) Thy two breasts, i. e., the corporeal and spiritual teachings (are) like two young twins, i. e., because the body and soul are created as one. (4:8) Come from Lebanon my sister bride, i. e., from Lebanon that was abundant in idols; he calls the soul his sister for his natural father is her father through
grace. Thou wilt come and passover from the top of Amanas, i. e., the mighty ones, from the top of Shenir and Hermon from lions' dens and from the mountains of the leopards, i. e., by this he indicates the heathen customs which were abundant in the world. (4:9) Thou hast inspirited me with one of thine eyes, i. e., with that spiritual one which is clear from white spots. With one chainlet of thy neck, i. e., easily wert thou bound to my yoke. (4:11) And the smell of thy garments is like the small of Lebanon, i. e., you are a daughter of many nations, not a daughter of one. (4:12) A garden that is closed, a fountain that is sealed, i. e., it will not again be violated by demons. (4:13) Thy plants are as an orchard of pomegranates, i. e., words of praise that you sent through the tongue of your messenger are well ordered and full of beauty. The Hebrew says thy mouth is a garden of pomegranates; nard, i. e., Roman nard. (4:14) Myrrh and aloes, i. e., aloes. They are the guardians of the body from the destroyer. (4:15) A fountain of gardens, i. e., spiritual spices, flowing from the soul, a well of living waters, i. e., divine teachings, that stream from Lebanon, i. e., from the heights above.

div.head: Section Two.
div.ab:
Section Two. (4:16) Awake, O north and come south, i. e., he calls to various nations to take pleasure in the
garden of the church; the Greek reads rise.

(5:2) I sleep, but my heart waketh, i. e., when I restrained the bodily senses my heart became light like that (saying) shut the windows that it may be light in the dwelling-place. For my head was filled with dew, i. e., the bridegroom makes known his incarnation, and my locks (are wet) from the drops of the night, i. e., you took on human form when error increased. (5:3) I have put off my coat, how shall I put it on, i. e., the old order of man. (5:4) My beloved puts out his hand from the hole, with a stopping of Beth, i. e., when he took on bodily form and he appeared to me through the physical eyes, we will turn to him. (5:5) And my fingers dropped with myrrh upon the handle of the locks, i. e., when I had mortified my body then my gate was opened to him. (5:6) My soul failed when he spoke(Lit.: at his speech), i. e., I forsook all of them and clung to him. I sought him but I could not find him, i. e., I did not attain Him as He is, for He is a being which is hidden from mind. I called him but he gave me no answer, i. e., as long as
you are bound with the body you can not perceive me. (5:7) They smote me and wounded me, i. e., passionate and covetous forces oppressed me because I had not yet separated myself from them, they took away my veil from me, the watchers of the wall, i. e., they stripped the cloak from me and my neck was bare, but I was not ashamed, for I became conscious of my love of the bridegroom. (5:8) I adjure you O daughters of Jerusalem, i. e., sanctified souls. (5:11) His head is like a stone, i. e., a precious one, which shines. His locks are straight, i. e., his ornaments are simple and not cunning. (5:12) Rivers of waters (with a Zeqafa of sin), i. e., running (water) that are bathing in milk, i. e., in learning. And sitting upon fullness, i. e., when two wells are mixed together. (5:14) A row of gold (with a Revoso of Kof and the last kof stopped) his belly is an ivory carving, i. e., the bone of an elephant which is white and firm and indestructable of sapphire, i. e., a vessel of sapphire, i. e., sky-blue. (5:15) His breasts are like that of the Lebanon, i. e., his heart, because of the right spiritual plants.

(6:4) And thou are more beautiful than Jerusalem; i. e., my holy city. (6:5) Turn away thine eyes from opposite me, for they have made me to flutter; i. e., do not look at
those who are at the opposite, that you might not abhor me. (6:8) There are sixty queens and eighty concubines and virgins without number; i. e., the Book of Kings says that he had three hundred concubines and these eighty are doubtless those who were sent to him from the royal courts, as out of the seven hundred noble (women) that he had sixty were princesses. And queens are here the type of people who choose for themselves virtue by their own will; and concubines are those that were subjugated to them by force, and virgins are those who are profane. (6:9) One is my innocent dove; i. e., she who utterly denied this world. One is she to her mother; i. e., to wisdom. (6:10) That looks like the morning, i. e., like light. (6:11) I went down into a garden of nuts; i. e., the garden is this world and nuts are people, whose beauty is not disclosed unless their bodies are broken. (6:12) I did not know myself, i. e., true knowledge is veiled in this world, in the chariot of the people who are prepared; i. e., who are expected to believe; the Greek says like the chariot
of Aminadab, i. e., not the son of Aminadab the head of the tribe of Judah, who sent a gift to the tabernacle in a chariot.

(7:1) Return, Return, O Shulamite; i. e., turn, turn, O thou full of peace, to me, and do not seek me in the material world (Lit.: in the garden of the corporeals). (7:2) How beautiful are thy feet in sandels, daughter of the prepared; i. e., thy movements are in rhythm. The Greek reads the daughter of Nadob, i. e., daughter of nobles. The form of thy thighs; i. e., thy ways of life are concealed like sections, the work of the hands of a cunning workman; i. e., by wisdom were they directed (with a Revoso of Sin) and (with a Zeqofo of Sin). (7:3) A round goblet, and drink is not lacking in it, thy belly (is like) a heap of wheat set about with lilies; i. e., drink and eat is a type of spiritual (food), as thus come eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed. (7:5) Thine eyes are (like) the
pools in Hesbon by the gate of the daughter of many, i. e., your look is thoughtful, and examines closely the results of actions. Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon; i. e., you breathe the high things. (7:6) Thine head upon thee is like carmel, i. e., exalted, like purple of the king which is bound with rows of stitching; i. e., the color of which shines upon water. (7:9) I said I will climb up unto the palm tree; i. e., I will be well pleased with your uprightness, and I will dwell in you. I am my beloved's and his turning is towards me (with a Zeqofo of Nun), i. e., his return. (7:13) Let us go forth into the field, let us lodge in the village, i. e., in the village of the world and we will see people who are producing good fruits. (7:14) And at our gates are all fruits new and old, i. e., both testaments are before our eyes.

(8:1) Suckled the breasts of my lambs, i. e., young souls. I will find thee in the streets, I will kiss thee and they will not despise me, i. e., for pure and holy is my love for you. (8:5) Who is this who cometh up from the wilderness, i. e., he is elevated to the height by means of reason. I stirred thee up under the apple tree, i. e., when you were engaged in corporeal desires, I scorned you for in them were you born. (8:7) Streams cannot sweep it away, i. e., temptations. (8:8) We have a little sister, i. e., a young soul, and she has no breasts, i. e., she has not yet gotten spiritual nourishment. In the day when she will be spoken for, i. e., when they will revile her. (8:9) If she is a wall we will build upon her pinnacles of silver, i. e., we will strengthen her with belief. And if she is a door we will enclose her with boards of cedar, i. e., we will adorn her with good and sincere manners, that is to say, we will make her comely in theory and practice. (8:10) I am a wall and my breasts like towers, i. e., because I was advanced in knowledge. (8:11) Solomon had a vineyard, i. e.,
the Messiah (had) the world and its fruit is plenty(abundant), i. e., wealth. Thou gave the vineyard over unto keepers to the superintendents of the church. A man gave for its fruits a thousand (pieces) of silver, i. e., Thou, O Lord, givest a plentitude of reward to those who fear Thee. The thousand are thine, O Solomon, i. e., those who love Thee do not ask another reward besides Thee. And two hundred to the keeper of the fruits, i. e., even the superintendents and teachers did participate in the reward. (8:14) Turn back my beloved, i. e., return to me, be like a roe, i. e., overtake me easily, upon the mountains of sweet spices, i. e., by pleasures which are loftier than this world.
End of the Book of Song of Songs.

noteGrp.note: p. 8, n. 1 The word = navel, for thigh quoted in chapter 7, verse 3, from the Peshitta and mentioned here is not to be found in the Peshitta texts. The Peshitta uses another word, but the meaning is the same.
p. 8, n. 2 Rashi on the first verse says, A song which is above all other songs dedicated to God by His congregation and nation, the Jewish people.
p. 9, n. 1 Perhaps materialists. Jerome calls literal translation Jewish. Farrar, p. 232.
p. 9, n. 2 Teshbhath Teshbhatha, the Syriac terms for the Song of Songs.
p. 9, n. 3 So has the Pol. (Lee's edition) and all the Hebrew texts known to us. This indicates that B. H. didn't use the Hebrew texts and so do we find numerous instances throughout his scholia.
p. 9, n. 4 Hippolytus....Denn die kinder saugen aus den Brusten Milch, so ein jeder saugend vom Gesetz der Gebote des Evangeliums..... Hyppolytus Werke, ed. Bomwetich and Achelis, p. 344.

p. 10, n. 1 This comment is found in the Midrash Rabah on this verse. It reads as follows, There is a difference between a person who was born hideous and one who was born comely but later became ugly, for it is easy for the latter to return swiftly to beauty, so said the Jewish people to the Gentiles, I am black, yet comely. And furthermore, said the Jews to the Gentiles, 'we will tall you to what we are likened, to a prince who went out to the desert and the sun beat down upon his head until his face became blackened. Then he came back to the city and with a little water and a little washing his body returned to its whiteness and he became once more comely. So are we when the sun of idolatry blackened us. But you are black from your birth, for even in your mother's womb you worshipped idols.

p. 10, n. 2 The subjugation of the corporeal forces to the soul is the main thought which B. H. stresses throughout his commentary to this book, and it is found in Maimonides Guide for the Perplexed which was originally written in Arabic. There he says (Friedlander, 2nd edition, pp. 395-96), The fourth kind of perfection is the true perfection of man.... whilst neglecting your soul till it has lost entirely its original purity through the dominion of the bodily powers over it. The same idea is expressed in the beginning of those poems, which are devoted to this subject my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept. Hippolytus says, Die sohne meiner mutter streiten mit mir, Der Teufel stritt mit uns.....
p. 11, n. 1 Rashi in his comment on this verse says, Reflect upon the ways of thy first fathers who received my Torah and observed my rules and commands, and travel in their paths.

p. 11, n. 2 1:9 This comment is very loosely attached to the Syriac text. It is only justified by the Hebrew word of the M. T., taken as a plural of , the law. A Midrashic ms. of a late origin found in the Genizah and issued by Dr. Grünhut (1897, Jerusalem) reads as follows:
p. 12, n. 1 The Midrash Rabah commenting on this verse expresses the same idea. As the dove is innocent, so is Israel.

p. 13, n. 1 Wine is frequently interpreted as a symbol for learning in the Midrashic literature. Also here the Midrash says, The Lord brought me into a great wine cellar, i. e., Mount Sinai. Also in Tractate Ta'anith 7a of the Babylonian Talmud - Why is the learning of the Torah compared to water, wine and milk?

p. 13, n. 2 A similar comment on this verse is found in the Midrash on Song of Songs (found at Genizah by Dr. Grunhut). It reads as follows: By the gazelles and by the antelopes of the field. The Lord said: I adjure you by the hosts that went out to Egypt and by the head of the tribes, that are compared to animals. (vide Genesis 4:9 where Jacob in blessing his sons, describes their qualities as compared with those of certain animals.) Jacob's sons, and the generation that went out of Egypt are considered in Midrashic literature as very pious.
p. 13, n. 3 The transliteration of the Hebrew does not indicate he knew Hebrew, for he might have used the Hexaplar.
p. 13, n. 4 Midrash Rabah - Behind our wall of Sinai.
p. 14, n. 1 Midrash Rabah - He looks forth at the windows, as it is said, And the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai.

p. 14, n. 2 Midrash Rabah - The winter has passed, that is the kingdom of the Cuthim (Samaritans) when entices the world and seduces it with her falsehoods (usually a synonym for idolatry). The same thing is expressed by Hippolytus, ....das eis ward weich....der Regen ist weg und dahin, hier denkt er an die Sturmahnliche Verwirrung des Gotzendienstes, welche damals im Lande war. - P. 365.
p. 14, n. 3 Lee's text hasn't this phrase.
p. 14, n. 4 The same idea is expressed in the Grunhut midrash. The time of pruning is come. The time for the destruction of the wicked has arrived.
p. 14, n. 5 Grunhut's midrash interprets this similarly: And the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land. This is Elija.
p. 15, n. 1 Hip. Die Fuchse sind die Teufel mit dem Ihrigen....die Verderberder Garten send die charactere der menschen, p. 366.
p. 15, n. 2 The word the day, in this passage is also interpreted by the Midrash (Grunhut) as referring to that last day.
p. 16, n. 1 In the day of his wedding, that is the giving of the Torah - Tractate Ta'anith 26b.
p. 16, n. 2 Probably I Cor. 11:15.
p. 17, n. 1 Hippolytus - Schnur' bedeutet die Richtigkeit, welche aus dem Herzen kommt. - p. 370.
p. 17, n. 2 Hip. - Wie der Granatapfel, welcher die geniessbare Frucht hinter der schale verbogen hat, so hat der mensch die Frucht Gottes. - Ibid.
p. 17, n. 3 B. H. differs here from the Peshitta texts of L. and U. in that he uses the traditional verse division instead of connecting this verse with the foregoing one as the Peshitta does.
p. 17, n. 4 Hip. - Zwei....die Seele und der Leib. - p. 371.
p. 18, n. 1 Yalkut says on this verse, The Torah is compared to water.

p. 19, n. 1 Rashi's comment on this verse is very similar, it is meant, I have already learned for myself other ways, I can no longer return to Thee. Also Midrash Rabbah on the second half of verse three says, I have washed my feet from the dirst of idolatry.
p. 19, n. 2 The person is not what might be expected from the context.
p. 20, n. 1 Hip. Und die Tochter von Jerusalem sind die Engel und Unschuldigne. - p. 359.
p. 20, n. 2 Midrash Rabbah, Bathing in milk -- these are the laws.
p. 21, n. 1 Yalkut on v. 2. of this chapter says, He went down into his garden, i. e., the world.
p. 21, n. 2 In Yalkut we find R. Jose the son of R. Jehuda says, whoever has not seen a nut thinks there is nothing in it but wood. When he breaks it he finds a quantity of food. So are the Jews.....

p. 22, n. 1 This allegorical interpretation of Shulamith as peace is a favorite one in the Midrash, as Shulamith, i. e., the people among whom the world's peace dwells, also the people who made peace between Me and My world, etc.

p. 22, n. 2 A similar interpretation is to be found in Tractate Mo-ed Katan 16b ....what is meant by the joints of thy thighs, why is the learning of the law compared to a thigh? To tell you that just as a thigh is concealed, so are the words of the law concealed.
p. 22, n. 3 Proverbs, 9:5.
p. 23, n. 1 Yalkut and Midrash on this verse, The fishpools in Hesbon in accountings that are decided with deliberation and thought.

p. 23, n. 2 Tractate Erubin 21b on this verse says If the vine hath budded these are Bible students, the vine-blossom be opened these are Mishna students, the pomegranates be in flower these the Gemara students.
p. 23, n. 3 Erubin 21b ....have you heard what the meaning of new and old is? ....these are the words of the Torah and these are the words of the Sopherim.

p. 24, n. 1 Tractate Pesachim 87a R. Johanan said this is Elam who has been privileged to learn but has not been privileged to teach. Much more clearly in the Midrash Rabbah on this verse R. Johanan explained those verses as meaning Sodom.... she has no breasts she has not sucked the commandments and the good deeds.
